meta.title: Who really said "That best portion of a good man's life, his little, nameless, unremembered acts of kindness and of love"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine Wordsworth: the lines appear in Tintern Abbey, the last poem in Lyrical Ballads (1798), page 203. The popular reworded version is not what he printed.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'That best portion of a good man's life, his little, nameless, unremembered acts of kindness and of love'?
meta.ogDescription: Really Wordsworth — Tintern Abbey, Lyrical Ballads (1798), p. 203. But the quote-site version rewrites his line, and one site prints "unencumbered."

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and traceable to the page. The lines close a verse paragraph in “Lines written a few miles above Tintern Abbey,” the final poem in Lyrical Ballads, with a Few Other Poems (London: J. & A. Arch, 1798), where they appear on printed page 203. What almost nobody quotes correctly is the wording — Wordsworth wrote “That best portion,” not “The best portion … is.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Lines written a few miles above Tintern Abbey, on revisiting the banks of the Wye during a tour
Lyrical Ballads, with a Few Other Poems (London: J. & A. Arch, 1798), page 203 — the closing poem of the volume
13 July 1798, the date carried on the poem’s own heading
Reprinted in Wordsworth’s collected Poems (1815), vol. 2, with the semicolon after “life” softened to a comma

source.excerpt:
But oft, in lonely rooms, and mid the din
Of towns and cities, I have owed to them,
In hours of weariness, sensations sweet.
Felt in the blood, and felt along the heart,
And passing even into my purer mind
With tranquil restoration:—feelings too
Of unremembered pleasure; such, perhaps,
As may have had no trivial influence
On that best portion of a good man’s life;
His little, nameless, unremembered acts
Of kindness and of love. Nor less, I trust,
To them I may have owed another gift,
Of aspect more sublime…
trail: The poem carries its own date line, “July 13, 1798,” and was added last to Lyrical Ballads, closing the volume ↗.
The title page of the first edition names no author at all: “LYRICAL BALLADS, WITH A FEW OTHER POEMS. LONDON: PRINTED FOR J. & A. ARCH, GRACECHURCH-STREET, 1798 ↗.”
The lines themselves sit on printed page 203 of that volume ↗, punctuated “a good man’s life;” with a semicolon. Project Gutenberg’s 1798 text ↗ agrees.
In the 1815 collected Poems ↗ Wordsworth prints “On that best portion of a good man’s life,” with a comma — the form the modern quotation follows.
Wikiquote ↗ lists the passage among its sourced Wordsworth quotations, under the poem’s own heading rather than in any disputed or misattributed section.

author.name: William Wordsworth
author.heading: Who was William Wordsworth?
author.bio: Born at Cockermouth in Cumberland on 7 April 1770, Wordsworth helped launch the Romantic age in English poetry with Lyrical Ballads (1798), written jointly with Samuel Taylor Coleridge — a volume that traded eighteenth-century poetic diction for the ordinary speech of ordinary people. “Tintern Abbey” was the last thing he added to it, composed in his head on a July walking tour and written down only when he reached Bristol. He was appointed Poet Laureate in 1843 and died at Rydal Mount on 23 April 1850.

misattribution.heading: Right poet, wrong words
misattribution.intro: The attribution is sound — this really is Wordsworth. What has gone wrong is the text. The version that circulates has been quietly rewritten into a self-contained aphorism, and at least one large quote site has corrupted the key word outright.

items.who: “The best portion of a good man’s life is his little…”
items.why: Wordsworth wrote “That best portion,” because the phrase is the object of “may have had no trivial influence on…” — it is not a sentence on its own. Goodreads, for instance, prints it as “The best portion of a good man’s life: his little, nameless unremembered acts of kindness and love” ↗, losing a comma and the second “of.”

Quotes.net renders the line with “unencumbered” in place of “unremembered” ↗, with no source given. It reverses the whole point: the acts matter to Wordsworth precisely because nobody, including the doer, remembers them.

items.who: Quoted as standalone advice about kindness
items.why: In the poem the acts are not a recommendation but a piece of evidence. The first-edition page ↗ shows the lines arriving at the end of a sentence about remembered landscape that “may have had no trivial influence” on them.

misattribution.truthLine: What the 1798 first edition actually prints, on page 203 ↗: “On that best portion of a good man’s life; / His little, nameless, unremembered acts / Of kindness and of love.”

context.heading: Why the lines are not actually advice
lead: Read on a poster, the lines sound like an instruction: be kind in small ways. In the poem they are doing something stranger. Wordsworth is describing what five years of carrying a remembered landscape in his head has done to him — “sensations sweet, / Felt in the blood, and felt along the heart” — and the little acts of kindness are not the advice, they are the evidence. The remembered Wye valley, he guesses, “may have had no trivial influence” on them.

That grammar is why the popular rewrite matters. Turning “That best portion” into “The best portion … is” snips the sentence free of the thing it was hanging from, and converts a tentative claim about where goodness quietly comes from into a flat maxim about what goodness is.
detailsBody: Wordsworth revisited the banks of the Wye on 13 July 1798, five years after an earlier visit — the poem opens by counting the gap: “Five years have passed; five summers, with the length / Of five long winters!”
“Tintern Abbey” was added last to Lyrical Ballads and printed as the closing poem of the 1798 volume, whose title page carries no author's name at all.

sourcesVerified.claim: The lines "On that best portion of a good man's life; / His little, nameless, unremembered acts / Of kindness and of love." appear on printed page 203 of the 1798 first edition of Lyrical Ballads.
The poem is titled "Lines written a few miles above Tintern Abbey, On revisiting the banks of the Wye during a tour" and carries the date line July 13, 1798, in the 1798 Lyrical Ballads.
The first edition's title page reads "LYRICAL BALLADS, WITH A FEW OTHER POEMS. LONDON: PRINTED FOR J. & A. ARCH, GRACECHURCH-STREET, 1798" and names no author.
Wordsworth's 1815 collected Poems, vol. 2, prints "On that best portion of a good man's life," with a comma, followed by "His little, nameless, unremembered acts / Of kindness and of love."

Project Gutenberg ebook 9622 is Lyrical Ballads, With a Few Other Poems (1798) by Wordsworth and Coleridge, and its text contains the passage "On that best portion of a good man's life; / His little, nameless, unremembered acts / Of kindness and of love."

Wikiquote lists the passage "that best portion of a good man's life, / His little, nameless, unremembered acts / Of kindness and of love" under its "Lines Written a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey" heading among sourced quotations, not under Misattributed or Disputed.
The poem was composed on 13 July 1798 during a walking tour of the Wye and was added at the last moment as the concluding poem of Lyrical Ballads (1798).
Lyrical Ballads was published by J. and A. Arch in 1798, and "Lines Written a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey" is the final entry in the first edition's poem list.

William Wordsworth was born 7 April 1770 at Cockermouth, Cumberland, died 23 April 1850 at Rydal Mount, served as Poet Laureate from 1843 to 1850, and helped launch the Romantic age with Lyrical Ballads (1798).
Goodreads displays the quote as "The best portion of a good man's life: his little, nameless unremembered acts of kindness and love.", credited to Lyrical Ballads.

Quotes.net prints the line as "The best portion of a good man's life is his little nameless, unencumbered acts of kindness and of love", using "unencumbered" instead of "unremembered" and giving no publication source.
The Internet Archive holds a scanned copy of Lyrical Ballads, with a few other poems, 1798, by William Wordsworth, in its Eighteenth Century collection.
